title: Quantum transport cost cones: exponent monotonicity, sharp operator-norm approximation and the sign of the centred cost
shortTitle: Quantum transport costs: noncommuting observables never help
oneLine: A conjecture on quantum transport cost operators is proved, a retraction shows that noncommuting observables never improve block-shaped approximations, and the best errors are exact: 1/(1 + 2^max(p,1)) for the simplest limiting cost, with the centred cost of one observable nonnegative exactly when p ≤ 2.
abstract: In classical optimal transport, moving a unit of mass from x to y often costs |x − y|^p. In the quantum theory of De Palma and Trevisan, transport between quantum states is carried out by a quantum channel, and an observable A gives the cost operator G_p(A) = |A ⊗ I − I ⊗ A^T|^p. Because a state can have positive cost of transport to itself, the self-costs are subtracted; the resulting centred cost is guaranteed nonnegative for quadratic costs. Bunth, Pitrik, Titkos and Virosztek conjectured that the cones C_p of finite sums of such costs, for observables with finitely many outcomes, grow with p; this would make their p-Wasserstein divergence well defined for p ≤ 2. This candidate proves the conjecture by transferring two classical facts about the real line to spectral blocks: the snowflake embedding of the line (Mendel and Naor) and Ball's finite-dimensional compression (as recorded by Deza and Laurent). Its main new tool is a positive, operator-norm-contracting retraction onto classical cones of distance arrays: noncommuting observables never help to approximate a cost that is constant on spectral blocks and vanishes on the diagonal blocks. With it, exact distances are computed: for every three-level cost; 1/(1 + 2^max(p,1)) for the orthogonal-pair generators of the limiting cone in dimension at least three; and half that for the worst trace-one element in finite dimension at least three. These are also the smallest uniform errors in pure-state transport values. For four or more levels a polygon lower bound is proved; it is exact for three levels, can be strict when p > 1, and is conjectured to be exact when p ≤ 1. For one observable with at least three eigenvalues, the centred cost is nonnegative on all pairs of states exactly when p ≤ 2, and for p < 2 the divergence obeys a relaxed triangle inequality with the sharp constant 2^(2/max(p,1) − 1). Limits: bounded observables only; the sign of the centred cost for several noncommuting costs with p > 2 is open. AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate; no external peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification is claimed.

keyResults: Theorem 2.1 (proof): for 0 < p < q < ∞, every cost G_p(A) of an observable with n distinct eigenvalues is a sum of at most n(n − 1)/2 costs G_q(B_r) of functions of A; hence C_p ⊆ C_q for 0 < p ≤ q ≤ ∞ (Conjecture 9 of Bunth, Pitrik, Titkos and Virosztek), using the snowflake embedding of the line (Mendel and Naor) and Ball's compression (as recorded by Deza and Laurent).

Theorems 2.2 and 6.1, Propositions 6.3 and 6.4 (proof): a positive, operator-norm-contracting projection maps every C_p onto a classical cone of distance arrays and fixes block-constant targets; noncommuting observables never improve their approximation, in operator norm, in pure-state transport values and, in finite dimension, in every unitarily invariant norm.

Theorems 7.2 and 8.2, Corollary 8.3 (proof): exact distances for every three-level cost; for dim H ≥ 3, dist(E_uv, C_p) = 1/(1 + 2^max(p,1)) (1/3 for p ≤ 1; 1/5, 1/9, 1/17 at p = 2, 3, 4); the worst trace-one element of the limiting cone is at half that distance in finite dimension d ≥ 3.

Propositions 7.5 and 7.6, Conjecture 7.7: a polygon lower bound for any number of levels, exact for three levels; strict for the spectrum 0, 1, 9, 10 with p = 3, q = 6 (bound about 6300.58, best single function about 9224.3); conjectured exact for p ≤ 1, supported by 226 random instances with p ≤ 1 (and 174 with p > 1) and 200 cut-cone linear programmes.

Theorem 5.2 and Corollary 5.3 (proof): for one observable with n ≥ 3 eigenvalues, the centred cost is nonnegative on all states if and only if p ≤ 2, equivalently G_p(A) ∈ C_2; for p < 2 the p-divergence satisfies d(ρ, ω) ≤ 2^(2/max(p,1) − 1)(d(ρ, τ) + d(τ, ω)), with a sharp constant.

narration: Quantum transport cost cones: an Evidence Press briefing. Optimal transport looks for the cheapest way to move one distribution of mass onto another, and moving a unit of mass often costs a power of the distance travelled. With power one the cost is the distance itself; with power two it is the squared distance, which punishes long moves. In the quantum version of De Palma and Trevisan, transport between quantum states is carried out by a quantum channel, and a cost operator built from a measurable quantity plays the role of the powered distance. A state can have a positive cost of transport to itself, so these self-costs are subtracted to give a centred cost, and that centred cost is only guaranteed to be nonnegative for quadratic costs. Bunth, Pitrik, Titkos and Virosztek asked whether the collections of cost operators grow as the power increases. If they do, every cost with power up to two is secretly a sum of quadratic costs, and their quantum Wasserstein divergence is well defined. This candidate proves that they do grow, by carrying classical facts about the real line, due to Mendel and Naor and to Ball, into the quantum setting. Its main new tool is a retraction that replaces any cost by one built only from the given measurement blocks, without moving further from a block-shaped target. The consequence is that noncommuting observables never help. With this tool the paper computes exact errors. In at least three dimensions, the simplest limiting cost, which charges one unit for moving between two perpendicular states, is exactly one third away from all costs with power at most one, one fifth away when the power is two, and one seventeenth away when it is four, and no choice of measurements does better. Finally, for a single measurement with at least three outcomes, the centred cost never goes negative exactly when the power is at most two, and below that threshold a relaxed triangle inequality holds with a sharp constant. There are limits. The growth result concerns measurements with finitely many outcomes. For four or more levels only a lower bound is proved, and for small powers its exactness is only conjectured. Position and momentum are not covered, and whether sums of several noncommuting costs keep the centred cost nonnegative above power two is still open. Evidence Press published this anonymous, AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate, and its review was internal, not peer review. This briefing uses an AI-generated voice and is not additional scientific evidence.

decisionObject.description: Treat quantum p-Wasserstein divergences of Bunth, Pitrik, Titkos and Virosztek as well defined for p ≤ 2, and compute best approximations of block-shaped cost operators with commuting (block) observables only.
decisionObject.scope: Observables with finitely many outcomes for the cone inclusions; bounded observables; exact distances for three levels and for the limiting-cone generators; only a lower bound for four or more levels; multi-observable sign question for p > 2 open.
